cities.d: the capital and largest city of the country

x.around: Minibuses are ubiquitous, cheap, and, if already full, fast. Single rides generally cost (about US$0.50). Most routes head to/from the 4 major bus stations in the city centre (referred to collectively as "town"), although there are a small number of alternative routes or short-cut routes, especially during the rush hours. A rider can get just about anywhere in the city with one connection in town.

hidden.d: Out in front of the Lusaka National Museum. The statue depicts a man breaking free of chains and is a reminder of Zambia's fight for freedom.
In the city showgrounds; holds exhibitions of local art. Unique and professional pieces are available and the staff will be happy to pack your work for safe travel.
It is an elegant concrete building with tall stained glass windows. Properly titled the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, it opened for worship on 14 September 1962.

n.en: Anglican Cathedral of the Holy Cross

hidden.d: A classic dusty, underfunded African museum that is worth a visit if you are at a loose end. An amusingly stark 'collection' of modern art on the ground floor, coupled with a more engaging exhibition upstairs covering Zambia's…
There's a nice crocodile pond here, murky waters and slithering serpents. And a swimming pool also.

Wildlife Park and Sanctuary, Botanical Gardens, Recreational Village and Environmental Education Centre. Started in 1956 as private garden and has grown to be Zambia's premier environmental education facility.
Some sticks and twigs here, maybe a duiker or something once in a blue moon. Place to let the kids out.

x.intro: Lusaka, in Lusaka Province, is the capital of Zambia. It is a cosmopolitan city that is home to about 2.7 million people (2020), approximately one in six Zambians. Lusaka is the centre of commerce and government in Zambia, and has several cultural facilities.

next.d: is on Lake Kariba about 2½ hours away from Lusaka

x.safe: Lusaka seems to have obtained a bad reputation for being a city plagued by crime, but in reality, this is exaggerated — other African cities such as Nairobi, Johannesburg and Lagos are much more risky. However, travellers should appreciate that walking around the city at night is foolish and that you will become a target for pickpockets if you make your valuables visible.

x.around: Chipata is strangely sprawling for a rural community. Most people with vehicles use them. For the most part, however, walking will be manageable, although possibly tiring.

hidden.d: Probably the prettiest building in Chipata, no entry for non-Muslims but just down the road from the Down Shops. Muslims only make up a relatively small minority of the population, however.

x.intro: Chipata is a growing multi-cultural town in Eastern Zambia, and is a popular refueling station for overlanders on their way east to Malawi, west to South Luangwa National Park, or north to Lundazi.

next.d: among the best in Zambia, also 2-3 hours away via Mfuwe

cities.d: large town midway between Lusaka and Ndola

x.around: In its heyday many of Kabwe's streets were paved and lighted. Today the light posts are still there but except for right in town the lights are all gone, and all but the main streets have deteriorated back into dirt roads with serious bumps and holes, so go slowly and carefully if you drive a car.

hidden.d: A very large fig tree that is a National Landmark. It has a small park with benches located under its shady leaves. This is the most common location for public events and promotions.

A national symbol, the Rock of Authority is called "the birthplace of Zambian independence". It was first used in 1958 for a rally of the Zambian African National Congress and then in 1960 for the first conference of the…

x.intro: Kabwe is a city in Central Zambia. It is the capital of Central Province.

cities.d: mining city in the Copperbelt and Zambia's second largest

hidden.d: Might be a good opportunity for spotting birds (paradoxically more prevalent during the hot season), or possibly waterback, monkeys, zebras, and tortoises.
There could be around 130 chimps living here at this sanctuary. You can try to see them during the feeding time or just any time with a guide. About 2 hours from Kitwe.

x.intro: Kitwe is large mining town in Northern Zambia, in the Copperbelt region.

x.around: The city of Livingstone, where the bulk of the accommodation, restaurants, nightclubs, etc. are, is relatively small. Most likely, you will be comfortable walking around town. However, if you prefer not to, taxis prowl constantly. Official taxis are ones which are blue and have a red number plate. If you flag a taxi down on your way to the town centre, the driver may ask whether you are booking the taxi or not.
x.intro: Livingstone is to Zambia what the town of Victoria Falls is to Zimbabwe. Formerly known as Maramba, it was the capital of Zambia before it was moved to Lusaka. Livingstone is in the Southern Province of Zambia and is the tourist capital of the country.

must.d: Has a natural history section, as well as an area describing the independence of Zambia from (naturally) a very Zambian perspective. There is a curio shop in the museum, and many touts out the front.

x.safe: Generally, Livingstone is a fairly safe town. They want to continue to attract foreign currency, so they are careful to make travellers feel safe. However, be careful about walking downtown at night, especially if you've been drinking. There are very few street lights, and many of the locals are very poor. Try not to annoy the taxi-drivers, particularly late at night when some have been drinking.

hidden.d: Exhibits on local mining industry, bird species, and ethnography. (For Non Zambian Residents not worth it).
Site of the plane crash that killed former UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld in 1961. There's a garden and a small museum dedicated to his life and the role of the UN.

x.intro: Ndola is a large city in the Copperbelt of northern Zambia, 10 km from the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo. With a population in 2023 of 587,716, Ndola is all about mining. It powered the Zambian economy until the 1970s, then the price of copper crashed while oil prices soared, and Zambia sank under huge debts. The city has diversified into limestone, and from 2005 the price of copper recovered, but with little visible benefit to Ndola.

intro: Zambia offers travelers some of the world's best safari opportunities, a glimpse into "real Africa", and Victoria Falls, one of the World's Seven Natural Wonders and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

other.d: largest national park of the country

x.intro: Kafue National Park is in the Kafue River Basin of Zambia. It is approx. 22,400 km² and is one of the largest parks in the country and the world. Its geography varies considerably from flood plains in the north to desert regions in the south.

other.d: used to be the president's private game reserve, now pristine wilderness without mass tourism
open for day trips and safaris

x.around: The bush camps and one lodge are self-suffient, operating their own airstrips, safaris, accommodation and meals.
x.intro: North Luangwa National Park is a national park in Eastern Zambia, a short flight away from South Luangwa National Park. It was until 2005 the domain of a limited number of safari operators who held a government concession. Since 2005, day visitors have been allowed.

other.d: one of Africa's great safari destinations

x.around: Most visitors tour South Luangwa by car, either on safari drives organized by their lodge, or by their own 4WD vehicle. If going on your own, there are plenty of trails but the signposting can be a little haphazard, so pick up a map from the gate.
x.intro: Considered to be one of the greatest wildlife sanctuaries in the world, South Luangwa National Park is one of Zambia's main draws. This park is centered on the Luangwa River and is home to one of Africa's largest concentrations of wildlife.

next.d: village just outside the park, with some attractions of minor interest
a short flight (or arduous drive) away, offers wilder game and fewer visitors.

x.safe: Walking in the bush at night is extremely dangerous, and lodges provide escorts to take their guests even around lodge grounds. Hippos, crocodiles, lions and buffalo kill many people every year — although the victims are mostly unfortunate locals, not tourists.
